prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength concept to clocks of unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: B013 is a clear invention in the sense I used in my March lecture, as reported by Tohoku: a prize for a discovery or invention, with the topic and the people responsible for the original work identifiable. The idea is specific and original (a trapping wavelength at which the light shift cancels for the clock transition, so that many atoms can be interrogated at once). It was followed by realizations that reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, and the consequences are measurable: tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the preparation of a redefinition of the second. It is the only shortlisted entry that all eight of us ranked, with seven placing it in the top three, and across the openings Danielsson, Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig and Pearce all describe the same two-person allocation (Katori for the concept and early strontium clocks, Ye for taking performance to the limit). I do not equate that breadth of support with merit, but the independent descriptions of the attribution agree, which is more than can be said for most other entries. Independent confirmation in several national laboratories makes the maturity question easy. My own opening first place, B015, I now treat as a subject-matter preference that no colleague shares and that I should not push, given how close it is to my own field.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap and incrementalism. The 2005 prize covered the optical frequency comb, and the 2012 prize covered the control of single trapped ions, so some will read optical lattice clocks as the next step in a metrology line rather than a new discovery. Ye's earlier comb-linked work also makes the framing delicate. The two-name allocation also leaves out contributors who built and compared the clocks (Lemonde and the Paris group, the German groups, the NIST and JILA team members, and the ion-clock pioneers), and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the practical payoff is still partly prospective. Against the Higgs entry, B013 is the less consequential discovery for physics as a whole; I prefer it because its attribution can be defended, not because its significance exceeds that of the Higgs observation.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first because the concept is clear and original, the realizations brought optical standards to about 1e-18, and the two-person configuration is natural, with timing helped by the 2005 comb prize that prepared the ground.
responses.response: I agree on the science and on the two names, and I would add that the 2005 prize is as much a risk as a help. A committee member who reads this as a continuation of combs and ion clocks will call it incremental. I think the answer is that the lattice scheme solved a different problem from either, the simultaneous interrogation of a large atom ensemble without light-shift error, but you should expect that objection and not treat it as settled. Where I differ slightly is on your suggestion that others need not be adjudicated: the Paris and German groups and the Boulder team members are a real part of why the clocks reached this level, and the citation should be worded around the invention and its realization, not claim sole authorship of every clock result.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs observation first as a new particle seen independently by two detectors that the 2013 prize did not cover, but concedes that credit across a collaboration of thousands is hard, that Della Negra is a strong alternative to the names he chose, and that the trio is open to dispute.
responses.response: I put the significance of the Higgs observation above that of B013 and I do not dispute your scientific case. My disagreement is about whether the prize can express it fairly. You, Johansson, Mehlig and Pearce each choose three of the same four names (Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee), and you omit Della Negra, Johansson and Mehlig omit Virdee, and Pearce omits Jenni. If four members who all support the discovery cannot agree who the three are, the committee will have trouble defending any of them, and a prize that omits one of the two experiments' founders invites the objection that it is honoring a role and not original work. Unless you can propose a rule that selects three names and that we can state in the citation, I would keep B001 as my first alternative and not my preference.

responses.point: Johansson ranks the Higgs observation first, says experimental recognition is overdue, and proposes two ATLAS leaders and one CMS leader while openly noting that leaving out Virdee is a judgment call. He also ranks circuit QED fifth and discloses a close link to it through WACQT at Chalmers.
responses.response: I agree that recognition of the experimental Higgs discovery is overdue, and I value that you state the arbitrariness of your trio plainly. Your own proposal shows the problem, because it leaves Virdee out, which leaves only one CMS name, and Danielsson and Pearce both keep Virdee, so the balance between the two experiments is itself disputed. On a separate point, I note that you and I are both at Chalmers and that you have flagged your proximity to B054. That entry is not part of my preferred configuration, so it does not bear on my choice, but I would ask that if B054 comes forward you not be the one to carry its scientific case, and I will treat my own closeness to B015 in the same way.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first, ranks magic-angle graphene second, and proposes only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero for B046, arguing that a fair configuration favors the prediction and the experiment, while acknowledging Bistritzer's role as co-author of the key paper.
responses.response: I agree that B013 deserves first place. I disagree with the narrowing of B046. Bistritzer and MacDonald wrote the decisive paper together, and a prize that credits the prediction without its first author would be hard to defend to the physics community, while Jarillo-Herrero's group alone made the experiment, with Cao as first author. If the committee takes B046 up, the credited names should be settled from the record, not by dropping the name that is least famous. My main concern about B046 remains timing: the pairing of theory and experiment is clean, but the origin of the superconductivity is still debated and the discovery is only about eight years old, so I list it as an alternative and not as a preference.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory first and the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp topological insulator entry third, arguing that the DMFT trio is conceptually clean and underlies the treatment of the Mott transition and correlated materials, and that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is the most coherent theory-plus-experiment set within the supplied names.
responses.response: I respect the DMFT argument, which is the strongest theory case on the list, but no other member ranked it and I cannot see how it advances in this round without new support. On B044 I share your concern that the supplied names omit Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang: since the HgTe experiment followed their proposal, a prize to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would credit the observation without the step that identified the material. Together with the 2016 prize on topological phases, I rank it below B013 and B046, although I accept that it has broad support in the openings.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the Higgs observation first, IceCube second and optical lattice clocks third, stating that he finds instrument-driven discoveries most compelling, and notes that recognition of the lattice clocks follows related metrology prizes in 2005 and 2012 and is not premature.
responses.response: We agree on B013's maturity, and I think your point that the 2005 and 2012 prizes make this the third of a metrology series cuts both ways. I take it as a sign the field is established, but others may take it as saturation. I would also not move IceCube above B013, because you yourself describe the source identification as still early and the credited trio as missing AMANDA-era contributors, so the discovery of a diffuse flux is secure while what is established about sources is limited.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see optical lattice clocks as a distinct invention or as a continuation of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether Katori and Ye alone adequately represent the people responsible, given the Paris, German and NIST/JILA contributions that are not in the credited names.
Whether the Higgs observation can be given a defensible three-name allocation; if it can, it may outrank B013 on significance.
My account of dates and individual roles is recalled from memory and not verified against primary sources.
statement.conflict_note: I am an electron microscopist and a past president (2024) of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy, so I have a close subject-matter link to B015 (aberration-corrected electron optics), my own opening first place; I should not advocate for it and would recuse myself from decisions on it, although no personal tie to Rose, Urban or Haider is documented in my profile. Göran Johansson is a fellow Chalmers professor, which is relevant only to his disclosed link to B054. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B013, B001 or B046, and none of Katori, Ye, Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee, Bistritzer, MacDonald or Jarillo-Herrero is a documented colleague.
